_comment: Speed run: wall-clock fit / transform / fit_transform for the stratum
QuantileTransformer against scikit-learn, over a rows x cols grid.
One qt_params dict, with two axes crossed into it: n_jobs and
output_distribution. n_jobs is the stratum-only thread fan-out over features
in transform; the plots draw one curve per value in the same figure, so set
the list to the counts worth comparing on your machine.
subsample = null means the fit kernel sees every row, which is what makes
the fit measurement a measurement. At scikit-learn's default of 10000 the
kernel never sees more than 10000 rows and fit cost stops growing with rows;
set it to 10000 for a run that reports the out-of-the-box behaviour instead.
output_distribution takes either a single string or a LIST, and a list is
swept like rows and cols: one run per value. normal routes transform through
the ndtri/ndtr rewrite, which is the path with something to prove; uniform
leaves scikit-learn's own per-feature function in place and so measures the
n_jobs fan-out alone. Unlike n_jobs it changes WHAT transform computes, so
the values do not share a figure -- each becomes its own parameter set, named
after the distribution, and the plot filenames carry that name
(rows_vs_time_cols100_normal_transform.png). Drop it to a single string to
halve the run.
Data shape (NaNs, ties, skew) belongs to config_correctness.json: it changes
what the result is, not how fast the code gets there. Omitting the data block
gives clean normal columns seeded from random_state.
MEMORY CEILING -- read before widening the grid. One matrix is rows x cols x 8
bytes and a cell holds several at once (the data, the train/test split, and
each implementation's transformed output): 100000 x 1000 is 0.8 GB per matrix,
1000000 x 1000 is 8 GB. Raising cols to 10000 is only viable against the
smallest row count.
